questionText: Listen to a tutorial in which a tutor advises a postgraduate student on refining her research methodology.
audioScript:
Situation: A doctoral tutor advises a master's student on improving the methodology of her dissertation on remote learning outcomes.
Tutor: So, Lena, your draft looks solid, but the methodology needs sharpening. Let's go through it.
Lena: Thanks. I'm using a mixed-methods approach: a survey of two hundred students plus fifteen follow-up interviews.
Tutor: Good. For the survey, have you considered selection bias? Your sample is drawn only from one university.
Lena: I see. Should I broaden it to two more institutions?
Tutor: Ideally yes. Triangulating across three universities strengthens the validity of your claims.
Lena: What about the interview schedule? Should it be semi-structured?
Tutor: Semi-structured is wise. It allows flexibility while keeping a consistent core of questions for comparability.
Lena: How long should each interview last?
Tutor: Aim for forty-five minutes. Shorter and you lose depth; longer and participants suffer fatigue.
Lena: Should I transcribe the recordings myself?
Tutor: Manual transcription improves familiarity with the data, but it's time-consuming. Consider software for a first pass.
Lena: For analysis, I plan thematic coding. Is that appropriate?
Tutor: Yes, thematic analysis suits qualitative data well. Use a framework like Braun and Clarke's six phases.
Lena: Finally, how do I address ethical concerns?
Tutor: Secure informed consent, anonymise all participants, and store data on an encrypted drive. Submit your ethics form by the end of the month.

audioScript:
Situation: A biology lab instructor meets a student to review his lab report investigating the effect of temperature on amylase enzyme activity.

Instructor: A labelled diagram of the active site would earn extra marks. Put it in the appendix, not the main text.
James: What about the conclusion?
Instructor: Keep it to one paragraph. State the optimum temperature and briefly mention the denaturation point. Avoid introducing new data there.

questionText: Listen to a supervisor advising a postgraduate student on planning a literature review on climate fiction.
audioScript:
Situation: A dissertation supervisor meets a postgraduate student to plan a literature review on climate fiction in contemporary novels.

Supervisor: Thematically. Organise it around three strands: representations of disaster, human-nonhuman relationships, and political agency.
Marcus: That's helpful. Do I need to discuss gaps in the literature?
Supervisor: Absolutely. Identifying a gap justifies your own research. I noticed you haven't covered Indigenous perspectives. That's a significant gap.
Marcus: You're right. I'll add a subsection on Indigenous climate narratives.
Supervisor: Good. Use a synthesis matrix to track sources against themes. It prevents a shopping-list style review.
Marcus: What referencing system should I use?
Supervisor: MLA ninth edition, since you're in literary studies. Be consistent with in-text citations.

questionText: Listen to a psychology lecturer helping a student design an experiment on the effect of sleep on memory.
audioScript:
Situation: A psychology lecturer meets an undergraduate student to design an experiment investigating the effect of sleep deprivation on short-term memory.
Lecturer: So, Daniel, your proposal is to test how sleep deprivation affects short-term memory. Let's refine the design.
Daniel: I plan to have three groups: a control group that sleeps eight hours, a group that sleeps four hours, and a group that is fully sleep-deprived for twenty-four hours.
Lecturer: Good start. How will you measure short-term memory?
Daniel: I was thinking of a word recall task, giving participants a list of twenty words and asking them to recall after two minutes.
Lecturer: A word recall task is standard, but consider adding a digit span test as well. It strengthens the validity by using two measures.
Daniel: That's a good idea. How many participants do I need per group?
Lecturer: For a study like this, aim for at least twenty per group, so sixty total. That gives you enough statistical power.
Daniel: Should I use a between-subjects or within-subjects design?
Lecturer: Between-subjects is more appropriate here. You can't ethically ask the same person to go without sleep for twenty-four hours repeatedly.
Daniel: Right. How do I control for individual differences in memory ability?
Lecturer: Administer a baseline memory test before the sleep manipulation and use it as a covariate in your analysis.
Daniel: What statistical test should I use to compare the three groups?
Lecturer: A one-way ANOVA, since you have one independent variable with three levels. If significant, run a post-hoc Tukey test.
Daniel: Are there any ethical approvals I need?
Lecturer: Yes, submit your ethics application to the committee. Participants must give informed consent and be able to withdraw at any time. Also, arrange a debriefing session afterwards.

questionText: Listen to an economics professor advising two students on preparing a presentation about inflation and monetary policy.
audioScript:
Situation: An economics professor meets two postgraduate students to review their upcoming presentation on the relationship between inflation targeting and monetary policy transmission.
Professor: Let's go through your presentation on inflation targeting. You have twenty minutes total. How have you divided it?
Nina: I'm covering the theoretical framework, about eight minutes. Ravi handles the empirical evidence, also eight minutes, and we leave four minutes for questions.
Professor: That's balanced. But Nina, your theoretical section is too broad. You're trying to cover five different models. Narrow it to two: the Taylor Rule and the New Keynesian Phillips Curve.
Nina: Understood. Should I include the Fisher equation?
Professor: Mention it briefly as context, but don't derive it. Your audience already knows it.
Ravi: For the empirical section, I'm using data from the Bank of England between two thousand and 2010 and two thousand and ten to 2023.
Professor: Good periodisation. But why split at 2010 specifically?
Ravi: I chose 2010 because quantitative easing became significant after the 2008 crisis, and its effects are visible in the later period.
Professor: Reasonable. But be precise: QE began in 2009 in the UK. Say 2009, not 2010, as the turning point. Your data can still start in 2010.
Ravi: I'll clarify that. Should I show regression results on a slide?
Professor: No, full regression tables are too dense for a presentation. Instead, show a scatter plot of inflation against the policy rate with a fitted line. It's visually compelling.
Nina: What about the Phillips Curve? Some argue it has flattened. Should we address that critique?
Professor: Absolutely. Address the flattening Phillips Curve debate in your conclusion. Cite Blanchard's 2016 paper as a key reference.
Ravi: How many slides should we use in total?
Professor: Aim for no more than twelve slides, including the title and references. Keep font size at twenty-four point minimum.
Nina: Should we provide a handout?
Professor: Not necessary, but prepare a one-page summary of key findings for anyone who asks. Don't distribute it unless asked.

questionText: Listen to an architecture critic reviewing a student's physical model of a community library design.
audioScript:
Situation: An architecture critic meets a final-year student to review his physical scale model of a proposed community library in a suburban setting.
Critic: So, Oliver, this is your model for the suburban community library. The overall massing is quite elegant. Tell me about your material choices.
Oliver: The facade is locally sourced timber cladding, and the structural frame is cross-laminated timber, or CLT. I wanted sustainability to drive the design.
Critic: Good instinct. CLT reduces the carbon footprint significantly. But I notice the roof is flat. Have you considered rainwater drainage?
Oliver: I've included a concealed gutter system along the north elevation. Rainwater feeds into an underground cistern for greywater reuse.
Critic: Clever. But at this scale of one to fifty, the gutter detail is invisible. You should include a detail drawing at one to ten to show it.
Oliver: I'll add that. What about the interior layout? I've placed the children's reading area on the ground floor near the entrance.
Critic: That's the right call. Accessibility for families is critical. However, the acoustics study area is directly above the children's zone. Sound transmission will be a problem.
Oliver: I could add acoustic baffling between floors. Would that be sufficient?
Critic: Acoustic baffling helps, but I'd go further. Specify a floating floor system with resilient mounts. It adds about eight percent to the floor cost but solves the issue properly.
Oliver: Noted. The site orientation places the main glazing on the south facade for natural light.
Critic: South-facing glazing risks overheating in summer. You need solar shading. Have you modelled brise-soleil?
Oliver: Not yet. I'll add horizontal brise-soleil louvres at forty-five degree angles.
Critic: Good. Just ensure the louvre spacing is calculated to block high-angle summer sun while admitting low-angle winter sun. Run a daylight simulation.
Oliver: What software should I use for that?
Critic: Use Ladybug for Grasshopper. It's industry-standard for daylight and solar analysis. Bring the results to our next review.

questionText: Listen to two art history students comparing two Renaissance paintings under their tutor's guidance.
audioScript:
Situation: Two postgraduate art history students compare two High Renaissance paintings with their tutor in a seminar room.
Tutor: Today we're comparing Leonardo da Vinci's Virgin of the Rocks, the London version, with Raphael's Madonna of the Meadow. Both date to around 1505 to 1506. What strikes you first?
Clara: The compositional structure. Leonardo uses a pyramidal arrangement, but the figures are set in a shadowy, mysterious grotto. Raphael places his Madonna in a luminous, open landscape.
Tutor: Good observation. The lighting is a key difference. What technique is Leonardo famous for here?
Daniel: Sfumato, the smoky blending of tones, especially around the faces and hands. It creates soft transitions without hard outlines.
Tutor: Correct. And how does Raphael's approach differ?

Situation: Two computer science undergraduate students discuss the efficiency of sorting algorithms with their professor during office hours.
Professor: So you've both been working on the algorithms assignment. Let's talk about the sorting algorithms you've implemented. Which ones did you compare?

Professor: Good selection. What were the average-case time complexities you observed?
Aiden: All three showed O of n log n for random input. But Quicksort degraded to O of n squared on the reverse sorted data when we used the last element as the pivot.
Professor: That's expected. What's the standard fix for that?

Situation: A sociology tutor helps a final-year student refine the design of a survey on urban housing insecurity in a supervision meeting.

Liam: I'd plan the differentiation more systematically from the outset rather than adapting mid-lesson.
Tutor: That's a strong reflective insight. For your written reflection, aim for one thousand five hundred words. Structure it using Gibbs' reflective cycle.
Liam: I'm familiar with Gibbs. Should I include evidence from lesson observations?

questionText: Listen to a dental tutor reviewing two students' clinical practice cases in restorative dentistry.
audioScript:
Situation: A dental tutor reviews two students' clinical practice cases in restorative dentistry, focusing on composite resin restorations.
Tutor: Fatima, Daniel, let's review your clinical cases. Fatima, you performed a Class II composite restoration on a lower left second molar. Walk me through your adhesive protocol.
Fatima: I used a total-etch technique with thirty-seven percent phosphoric acid for fifteen seconds, then applied a two-step etch-and-rinse adhesive.
Tutor: Fifteen seconds on dentine may be too long. Over-etching can degrade the collagen network. Try ten seconds next time.
Fatima: I see. Should I consider a self-etch adhesive for posterior restorations?
Tutor: A self-etch system can reduce post-operative sensitivity, but bond strengths to enamel are generally lower. It's a clinical judgement call.
Daniel: For my case, I placed a Class I restoration on an upper right first molar. I used bulk-fill composite to save time.
Tutor: Bulk-fill materials can be placed in increments up to four millimetres. Did you verify the depth of cure?
Daniel: I didn't. How should I check that?
Tutor: Use a scrape test on the base of the increment. If the material is still soft, the cure is inadequate and you must layer it.
Fatima: What about the finishing and polishing stage? I found that challenging.
Tutor: Use a fine diamond bur for contouring, followed by aluminum oxide polishing points. Avoid coarse abrasives on the marginal ridge.
Daniel: How do we minimise polymerisation shrinkage at the margins?
Tutor: Employ an incremental layering technique with two-millimetre oblique increments. This reduces the C-factor and stress at the adhesive interface.
Fatima: Should we use a rubber dam for all posterior composites?
Tutor: Best practice is yes. Moisture control is critical for adhesive dentistry. Even slight saliva contamination can compromise the bond.
Daniel: When is our next clinical assessment?
Tutor: Your competency assessment is on the twenty-fifth of May. Bring your case portfolios with radiographs and photographs.

questionText: Listen to a pharmacy student discussing a drug interaction study with her supervisor.
audioScript:
Situation: A final-year pharmacy student reviews the design of her drug interaction study with her clinical supervisor.
Supervisor: Right, Priya, let's go through your protocol for the warfarin-amoxicillin interaction study. How many participants are you recruiting?
Priya: I'm aiming for one hundred and twenty patients across two hospitals.
Supervisor: Good. And what is the study duration you've proposed?
Priya: Six weeks of observation, with a two-week follow-up after the antibiotic course ends.
Supervisor: Sensible. Which primary outcome measure are you tracking?
Priya: The main endpoint is the change in INR readings, that's the international normalised ratio, within the first week.
Supervisor: Correct. INR is the gold standard here. What's your control group?
Priya: Patients on warfarin who are prescribed a non-interacting antibiotic, cephalexin, as the comparator.
Supervisor: Solid choice. How will you handle participants who miss doses?
Priya: We log missed doses in an electronic diary and exclude anyone who misses more than two consecutive days.
Supervisor: Pragmatic. And the statistical test?
Priya: I'll use a paired t-test for within-group comparisons and a Mann-Whitney U test between groups since the data may not be normally distributed.
Supervisor: Good thinking on non-parametric fallback. What's the main ethical consideration?
Priya: Since warfarin monitoring is standard care, we rely on a waiver of consent for data review, but full consent for any additional blood draws.
Supervisor: Exactly. Submit your ethics amendment by the fifteenth and we can begin recruitment next month.

Situation: Two agriculture students consult their lecturer about designing a four-year crop rotation plan for a dairy farm.
Lecturer: So, Tom and Megan, you're planning a rotation for the Watson dairy farm. What's the total arable area?

Lecturer: Good. What's the first crop you'd plant in year one?

Lecturer: Correct. What goes in year three?
Megan: We put in a legume, field beans, to fix nitrogen naturally and reduce fertiliser costs.

Lecturer: Good. What's the main risk of shortening the rotation to three years?
Tom: Build-up of soil-borne pests like take-all and cyst nematodes, which thrive without a sufficient break.

questionText: Listen to two meteorology students discussing a weather forecasting model with their professor.
audioScript:
Situation: Two postgraduate meteorology students discuss the limitations of a regional numerical weather prediction model with their professor.
Professor: Right, Sam and Olivia, you've been running the WRF model for the south-west region. What horizontal resolution are you using?
Sam: We've set it to four kilometres, which balances detail and computational cost.
Professor: Reasonable. What's the main issue you've found with the convective precipitation forecasts?
Olivia: The model tends to over-predict light rain events, producing false alarms on roughly thirty per cent of days.
Professor: That's a known bias. Which parameterisation scheme are you using for cumulus convection?
Sam: The Kain-Fritsch scheme. We chose it because it handles deep convection well in this climate.
Professor: Good. Have you tried the Grell-Freitas scheme as an alternative?
Olivia: Not yet. We plan a sensitivity run next week comparing the two schemes over a forty-eight-hour window.
Professor: Sensible. What's your verification metric?
Sam: We're using the equitable threat score for precipitation thresholds above one millimetre per hour.
Professor: Good choice. How long is your simulation period?
Olivia: Thirty days of the monsoon season, from the first to the thirtieth of July.
Professor: Adequate. What data are you using for initial and boundary conditions?
Sam: We downscale from the GFS global model at zero-point-five-degree resolution.
Professor: Fine. Finally, what's the biggest limitation you've identified?
Olivia: The model under-resolves orographic rainfall over the coastal ranges because the terrain is smoothed at four-kilometre grid spacing.

Hana: I ran an independent samples t-test on the Euclidean distance between the two vowel categories.
Tutor: Appropriate. What's the main limitation of your study?
Hana: The sample is urban only, so I can't generalise to rural Pacific Northwest communities.
Tutor: Fair point. What would you add in a follow-up?
Hana: I'd include reading-style and conversational-style tasks to test for style-shifting effects.
Tutor: Good. Finally, which theoretical framework are you using to interpret the change?
Hana: I'm using Labov's principles of chain shifting, specifically the prediction that low back vowels merge before front vowels raise.
